topic.subject: science
topic.title: Magnetic effects of electric current
topic.scope: magnetic field lines, field around a wire and solenoid, force on a conductor, domestic circuits, short circuit, earthing

misconceptions.statement: Magnetic field lines are real physical threads that exist around a magnet.
misconceptions.why: Students take the visual representation in diagrams literally as physical objects.
misconceptions.fix: Field lines are imaginary lines used to represent the direction and strength of the magnetic field.

probe.question: If you move your hand through a magnetic field, why don't you feel the lines snapping?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the lines are too thin or made of energy.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is drawn must exist physically
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Magnetic field lines can cross if two very strong magnets are brought close together.
misconceptions.why: Students think strength can overcome the rule of non-intersection.
misconceptions.fix: Field lines never intersect because the magnetic field at any point has only one unique direction.

probe.question: What would a compass needle do if it were placed at a point where two field lines crossed?
probe.wrong_answer: It would point in two directions at once or spin.

misconceptions.root_belief: more force can break physical rules

misconceptions.statement: The Right-Hand Thumb Rule is used to find the direction of the force on the wire.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between different hand rules (Thumb vs Left-Hand).
misconceptions.fix: The Right-Hand Thumb Rule is only for finding the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor.

probe.question: You want to find which way a wire will move in a magnetic field. Which rule do you use?

misconceptions.root_belief: one rule applies to all hand gestures

misconceptions.statement: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is zero because it is an empty space.
misconceptions.why: Belief that fields require a medium or a solid core to exist.
misconceptions.fix: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform and strong, represented by parallel straight lines.

probe.question: Describe the magnetic field at the very center of a long current-carrying solenoid.
probe.wrong_answer: There is no field because there is no iron core there.

misconceptions.root_belief: empty space cannot contain physical properties

misconceptions.statement: In Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, the thumb represents the direction of the magnetic field.
misconceptions.why: Arbitrary assignment of fingers due to lack of mnemonic practice.
misconceptions.fix: The thumb represents the Force (Motion), the forefinger represents the Field, and the middle finger represents the Current.

probe.question: Using the Left-Hand Rule, which finger points toward the North pole of the external magnet?

misconceptions.statement: The earth wire is used to complete the circuit so the appliance can turn on.
misconceptions.why: Confusing the function of the neutral wire with the earth wire.
misconceptions.fix: The earth wire is a safety measure that provides a low-resistance path for leakage current to the ground.

probe.question: Will a toaster work if the earth wire is disconnected but live and neutral are connected?

misconceptions.root_belief: all wires in a plug serve the same purpose

misconceptions.statement: A short circuit happens when the length of the wire in the circuit is too short.
misconceptions.why: Literal interpretation of the everyday word 'short'.
misconceptions.fix: A short circuit occurs when the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact, causing resistance to drop to nearly zero.

probe.question: Why does a short circuit cause a fire?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the electricity doesn't have enough room to travel in the short wire.

misconceptions.root_belief: scientific terms mean their everyday definitions

misconceptions.statement: A fuse 'creates' more power when the appliance needs it.
misconceptions.why: Misunderstanding the fuse as a source of energy rather than a breaker.
misconceptions.fix: A fuse is a safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit.

probe.question: What happens to the wire inside a fuse during an overload?
probe.wrong_answer: It expands to let more current through.

misconceptions.root_belief: components are active providers of the main effect

misconceptions.statement: A magnetic field exerts a force on any charge, even if it is standing still.
misconceptions.why: Overgeneralizing the interaction between magnets and charges.
misconceptions.fix: A magnetic field only exerts a force on a moving charge or a current-carrying conductor.

probe.question: A stationary electron is placed in a strong magnetic field. What is the force on it?
probe.wrong_answer: It will move towards the North pole.

misconceptions.root_belief: fields affect everything in their vicinity equally

misconceptions.statement: The magnetic field is strongest at the center of a bar magnet.
misconceptions.why: Intuition that the 'heart' or center of an object is its most powerful part.
misconceptions.fix: The magnetic field is strongest at the poles where the field lines are most crowded.

probe.question: Where will a bar magnet pick up the most iron filings?
probe.wrong_answer: In the middle of the magnet.

misconceptions.root_belief: the center is the source of power
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: A solenoid only has a magnetic field if it has an iron core inside it.
misconceptions.why: Confusing a solenoid with an electromagnet.
misconceptions.fix: A solenoid produces a magnetic field whenever current flows through it; an iron core only increases the field strength.

probe.question: Does a coil of copper wire produce a magnetic field when connected to a battery?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because copper is not magnetic.

misconceptions.statement: Overloading and short circuit are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both lead to the fuse blowing and involve high current.
misconceptions.fix: Overloading is connecting too many appliances to one socket; a short circuit is the direct contact of live and neutral wires.

probe.question: If you plug five heaters into one extension cord, is that a short circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the wires will get hot and touch.
